clue.text: She has pain in both sides

indicators.note: a word sitting in both sides is flanked by the abbreviations for the two sides, one at each end

parts.note: R and L, right and left, the two sides
an ache is a dull pain

explanation.surface: A woman suffers aches on both sides of her body.
explanation.walkthrough: ACHE goes between R and L to make RACHEL.
explanation.definitionFit: Rachel is a woman's given name, so the pronoun stands for a female person carrying it.

clue.text: Blame a financial centre for greed

parts.note: to take the rap is to take the blame
taken as written
the City is London's financial district

explanation.surface: Someone holds the banking world responsible for avarice.
explanation.walkthrough: The City (capital C) is the City of London, home of British banking.
explanation.definitionFit: Rapacity is grasping, insatiable desire for wealth, a close synonym of avarice.

clue.text: Hard case training for party activity

indicators.note: training puts something into a new shape, so these letters are drilled into another order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A tough guy is being schooled to join in at a party.
explanation.definitionFit: Charades is a parlour game of miming words, traditionally played at Christmas gatherings.

clue.text: A salt course?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the town gives its name to ... salts, magnesium sulphate
second meaning: the Surrey racecourse where the Derby is run

explanation.walkthrough: Read as one phrase it suggests a dose of salts or a seawater cure; Epsom salts are a purgative, and Epsom Downs is a famous English racecourse.
explanation.definitionFit: The Surrey town names both a well-known bath and purgative salt and a racing venue hosting the Derby.

clue.text: Frequently a couple of papers are taken on a round

parts.note: O is round in shape
the FT (Financial Times) and The Times, two newspapers

explanation.surface: A paperboy regularly takes two newspapers along on his delivery route.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taken on' means the papers come after the O.
explanation.definitionFit: Ofttimes is an archaic adverb meaning often, many times over.

clue.text: When new fried fish are cooked, one likes the window open

indicators.note: cooking transforms its ingredients, so these letters are worked into a new arrangement

parts.note: N is the standard abbreviation for new
taken as written
taken as written; the verb of the surface joins the mix

explanation.surface: Frying fish makes a smell, so someone opens the window.
explanation.walkthrough: 'When' and 'are' read as grammar in the surface, but 'are' is part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A fresh-air fiend is someone obsessed with ventilation and outdoor air, hence opening windows.

clue.text: Attempted to hold bend at speed and was successful

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it inside, so one word wraps around the others

parts.note: tried means attempted
a U-bend, shaped like the letter
miles per hour, a measure of speed

explanation.surface: A driver took a corner fast and came through it in one piece.
explanation.walkthrough: The U-bend is the plumber's bend shaped like the letter; MPH, miles per hour, is the usual crossword speed.
explanation.definitionFit: To triumph is to win or prevail, so triumphed is the past tense of succeeding.

clue.text: Women's movement has little insurrection

parts.note: the Mothers' Union, a Christian women's organisation
tiny means little

explanation.surface: A feminist campaign stages only a small uprising.
explanation.walkthrough: The Mothers' Union is a long-standing Anglican women's organisation, abbreviated MU.
explanation.definitionFit: A mutiny is a revolt against authority, especially by sailors or soldiers against officers.

clue.text: A pen was the first to be so described

definitions.text: A pen was the first to be so described

parts.words: A pen was the first to be so described
parts.note: surface reading: a pen being the first thing ever written about in a particular way; setter's reading: a style is an old word for a pointed writing tool, so a pen was the first thing named with this word, and named is the meaning

explanation.surface: A writing instrument was the first thing ever given a particular description.
explanation.walkthrough: A style or stylus was the ancient writing implement; the verb from it means called or named.
explanation.definitionFit: Styled means named or designated, and the noun it comes from originally meant a pointed writing implement.

clue.text: Gathering of spare fruit

indicators.note: a gathering collects things up in a new order, so these letters are regrouped

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Picking up the windfall fruit nobody needs.
explanation.definitionFit: Pears are orchard fruits, so the plural noun is an example of the general category.

clue.text: Go after a short skirt — it's a science

indicators.note: something short has been cut, so its final letter is dropped

parts.note: a chemise is a loose shift or slip
to have a go is to try

explanation.surface: Chasing a girl in a miniskirt is a matter of attraction, a science of sorts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go after' looks like the chase; 'go' is the piece and 'after' places it at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Chemistry is the branch of natural science dealing with substances and their reactions.

clue.text: Grass-roots TV audience

parts.note: surface reading: ordinary viewers at the base of society; setter's reading: the underground parts of couch grass, read as tubers of a lawn weed

explanation.walkthrough: Couch is a weedy grass, and potatoes are roots of a sort; together they make the slang name for lazy viewers.
explanation.definitionFit: Couch potatoes are idle people who spend long hours sitting watching television.

clue.text: Spell out "Hindhead" in Dorset

parts.note: a charm is a magic spell
taken as written
read as 'hind head': the head, or first letter, of hind

explanation.surface: Instructions to write out the name of a place called Hindhead, as if it lay in Dorset.
explanation.walkthrough: Hindhead is in fact a village in Surrey, which makes the surface a geographical tease.
explanation.definitionFit: Charmouth is a coastal village in Dorset, on the Jurassic Coast near Lyme Regis.

clue.text: It's seldom man gets infected with an animal ailment

indicators.note: an infection lives inside its host, so the answer is carried within the clue's words

parts.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: A reassurance that people rarely catch a disease from animals.
explanation.definitionFit: Mange is a skin disease of mammals caused by parasitic mites, causing hair loss.

clue.text: Viola player's busy time?

parts.note: surface reading: a musician who plays the viola at a hectic stage of the season; setter's reading: an actress taking the part of Viola, Shakespeare's heroine

explanation.walkthrough: Viola is the shipwrecked heroine of Shakespeare's comedy, so the actress playing her is busiest during its performances.
explanation.definitionFit: The Shakespeare play whose heroine is Viola, so its run keeps that actress fully occupied.

clue.text: Battleground — stage for salesman to make a killing?

definitions.text: stage for salesman to make a killing?

parts.note: the front is where battle is fought
a step is a stage in a process

explanation.surface: A war zone becomes a platform where a seller strikes it rich.
explanation.walkthrough: The doorstep salesman makes his killing, a big profit, standing at the house's entrance.
explanation.definitionFit: The step outside a house's main entrance is where door-to-door sellers make their pitch.

clue.text: In happy state of having space adequate for working

parts.note: an en is a printer's unit of space
viable means workable, able to function

explanation.surface: Someone content because they have enough room to work in.
explanation.walkthrough: An en (and an em) are typesetters' measures of space, common in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: Enviable describes a position others would covet, a fortunate, desirable situation.

clue.text: Teen rave as a new form of worship

indicators.note: a new form is a reshaping, so these letters take a fresh arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Young people's dance parties are becoming a modern religion.
explanation.definitionFit: To venerate is to regard with deep reverence, a verb synonym of worshipping.

clue.text: Motion that could lead to a fall

definitions.text: Motion that could lead to a fall

parts.words: Motion that could lead to a fall
parts.note: surface reading: a physical movement that might make someone trip; setter's reading: a parliamentary proposal whose passing can bring down a government

explanation.walkthrough: In Parliament a motion is a formal proposal; if this one passes, the government usually falls.
explanation.definitionFit: A vote of no confidence is a parliamentary motion that, when carried, forces a government to resign.

clue.text: Trollope's legal coterie

definitions.note: short for Trollope's county, the answer is a place name

parts.note: the Bar is the legal profession of barristers
a set is a clique or circle

explanation.surface: The novelist Trollope's circle of lawyer friends.
explanation.walkthrough: Anthony Trollope set his Chronicles of Barsetshire in an imaginary English county, Barset for short.
explanation.definitionFit: Barset is the fictional cathedral county in which Anthony Trollope set a series of novels.

clue.text: Extent of French endless 1 down

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter is dropped

parts.note: de is French for of
the answer to 1 down is rapacity, another word for this

explanation.surface: Asking how far the French go in avarice.
explanation.definitionFit: Degree means extent or level, as in 'to some degree', meaning to some extent.

clue.text: With drink it's right to be taking notice

parts.note: ale is beer
RT is an abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A tipsy claim that having a drink makes you more attentive.
explanation.definitionFit: Alert means watchful and wide awake, attentive to what is happening.

clue.text: Laxative taken mistakenly — in private, that is

indicators.note: done mistakenly means set down wrongly, so these letters are out of order

parts.note: taken as written
i.e., Latin id est, means that is

explanation.surface: Someone took a purgative by accident, which is best kept quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' puts 'that is' among the letters of 'private' before the whole lot is rearranged; aperitive is a rare word, kin to aperitif.
explanation.definitionFit: Aperitive is an old adjective and noun for something opening the bowels, a mild purgative.

clue.text: Religion requires one to distribute alms

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: distributing spreads things around, so these letters are dealt out afresh

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A faith obliges its followers to give charity.
explanation.walkthrough: Almsgiving (zakat) really is one of the Five Pillars of the faith, so the surface is true.
explanation.definitionFit: Islam is the monotheistic faith founded through the Prophet Muhammad, one of the world's major religions.

clue.text: Cultural centre backs arts with model car

indicators.note: something going backs-first is turned round, so the word is read from its end

parts.note: taken as written
the Model T Ford, an early mass-produced car

explanation.surface: An arts venue sponsored by a carmaker.
explanation.walkthrough: Stratford-upon-Avon is Shakespeare's birthplace and home of the Royal Shakespeare Company.
explanation.definitionFit: Stratford-upon-Avon is a major centre of theatre, as the home of the Royal Shakespeare Company.

clue.text: Sign of Blair embarrassment?

indicators.note: embarrassment is confusion, so these letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A telltale indication that the Prime Minister, Tony Blair, is red-faced.
explanation.definitionFit: Libra, the scales, is one of the twelve signs of the zodiac.

clue.text: Lock spring breaks giving uninvited access

indicators.note: breaking into something means getting inside it, so one word goes within the other

parts.note: a tress is a lock of hair
a spa is a mineral spring

explanation.surface: A burglar snaps a lock's spring to get into a house uninvited.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lock' and 'spring' look like door hardware; they are hair and water.
explanation.definitionFit: Trespass is entry onto another person's property without permission or right.

clue.text: A politician before, Andre's currently a physicist

parts.note: taken as written
a Member of Parliament
ere is an old word for before

explanation.surface: A former MP named Andre has become a scientist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Currently' puns on electric current: André-Marie Ampère's name lives on as the unit of current.
explanation.definitionFit: André-Marie Ampère was the French physicist who founded electrodynamics; the unit of electric current honours him.
